title: Bigger, Better, More
overview: Compare things, places and prices: cheaper, more comfortable, the best. Say how you do things: well, hard, badly. Ask How much? and How many?, and Which one is yours? Read and say numbers up to 1,000.
learningPath: The lesson: listen, repeat and say it.
Words: listen, look and say. 24 words.
Patterns: 6 cards. Read the one done for you first.
Reading: read 3 texts and answer the questions.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, then listen back.
Writing: 4 short texts. Made-up answers are OK.
Practice: 6 exercises. Check with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. Last, go to My progress.
lectureScript:
Hello! This is Unit 17.
In this unit, you compare things.
You say which one is cheaper, bigger or better.
Listen.
The bus is 3. The taxi is 20.
The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
Cheap, cheaper. A short word takes -er.
Then say than, and the other thing.
My bag is lighter than your bag.
Heavy, heavier. The y becomes i.
Big, bigger. Two g.
A long word takes more.
The taxi is more expensive than the bus.
This chair is more comfortable than that chair.
Use -er or more, never both.
Not: more cheaper.
Now three things, or more.
The bus is the cheapest.
The taxi is the most expensive.
Short word: the -est. Long word: the most.
Two words change. Listen.
Good, better, the best.
Bad, worse, the worst.
This café is good. That café is better.
The café on the corner is the best.
Far changes too: far, further, the furthest.
The station is further than the market.
Say what you think with I think.
I think the train is better.
Now, how you do things.
She is a quiet person. She talks quietly.
Most how words end in -ly.
But good changes. It becomes well.
She is a good cook. She cooks well.
Hard stays hard. He works hard. Not hardly.
Bad becomes badly. I sing badly.
Now, how many and how much.
You can count eggs.
How many eggs do you need?
You can't count rice.
How much rice do you need?
I need a kilo of rice. I need two litres of milk.
A lot of is for both.
I need a lot of eggs. I need a lot of rice.
Many and much are for questions, and for not.
There aren't many eggs. There isn't much milk.
Use some in a yes sentence. I've got some bread.
Use any in a question, and with not.
Have you got any milk? No, I haven't got any milk.
No means not any. There is no milk.
For a price, ask: How much is it?
It is 45.
Now, which one.
There are two bags. Which one is yours?
This one. It is near me.
That one. It is not near me.
Say one. Do not say bag again.
Last, big numbers.
One hundred. A hundred and five.
Two hundred and fifty.
Say and after hundred.
After a number, hundred has no s.
Three hundred. Not three hundreds.
Ten hundreds is a thousand.
One thousand.
The price is 450. Four hundred and fifty.
The bag is 750 grams. Seven hundred and fifty grams.
Now you. Look at two things near you.
Say which one is bigger.
Say which one you think is better.
It can be true or made up.
Now go to Words. Goodbye!

outcomes.outcome: Compare two things in writing with -er or more and than, compare three or more with the -est or the most, and write which one you choose.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 1 practice self-checked; Practice 1, eight items; Writing 1 and Writing 4 checklists; Quiz items 1 to 3.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write: The bus is cheaper than the taxi.

outcomes.outcome: Say which of two or three things is better, the best, worse or the worst, and say what you think with I think.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 practice; Practice 2; Speaking 1 recording; Writing 4 line 4; Quiz items 4 and 5.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say: I think the green bag is better.

outcomes.outcome: Say how you do things with quietly, well, hard and badly, and use good for a thing and well for how you do it.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 3 practice; Practice 3; Speaking 2 recording; Writing 2 checklist; Quiz items 6 and 7.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say how I do things: I cook well. I sing badly.

outcomes.outcome: Ask and answer about amounts and prices with How many, How much, some, any, a lot of and no.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 4 practice; Practice 4; Speaking 5 recording; Writing 3 checklist; Quiz items 8 and 9.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can ask: How much is it? How many eggs do you need?

outcomes.outcome: Ask and answer Which one is yours? and Which one do you want? with this one, that one and the red one.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 5 practice; Speaking 6 role-play recording; Writing 4 line 5; Quiz item 10.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can ask Which one is yours? and answer This one.

outcomes.outcome: Read, write and say numbers up to 1,000 in prices, sizes and measures, and find what you need on a price list.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 6 practice; Practice 5 and Practice 6; Reading 2 and 3 questions; Speaking 4 recording; Quiz items 11 and 12.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can read a price list and find the price I need.

outcomes.outcome: Listen to two people compare things, and say which one each person likes or thinks is better.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 3 answers checked against the key; Reading 1 questions 1 and 4, heard and read.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can hear which one a person thinks is better.

words.meaning: Big. Shops often use it for sizes.
words.example: Can I have a large coffee, please?
practice: The large bag is 40. The small one is 25.
This room is larger than my kitchen.
Large, larger, the largest.
It is the largest park in the city.
What size do you want, small or large?
words.tutor: Name three things in your home to the tutor. Say which one is the largest. Ask it to check how you spelled largest.

words.meaning: You can't carry it easily. It has a lot of kilos.
words.example: This box of books is heavy.
practice: My bag is heavier than your bag.
Heavy, heavier, the heaviest: the y becomes i.
The big bottle of water is the heaviest.
Is the box heavy? Yes, it is. Can you help me?
words.starter: The heaviest thing in my room is …
words.tutor: Tell the tutor two things you carry every day. Say which one is heavier. Then type heavier, and ask the tutor to check the i.

words.meaning: Not heavy. You can carry it easily.
words.example: My new phone is very light.
practice: A light bag is good for a trip.
The green bag is lighter than the black bag.
This is the lightest chair in the shop.
Light, lighter, the lightest: the gh is quiet.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three pairs of things, like a pen and a book. For each pair, say which one is lighter.

words.meaning: You can do it with no help.
words.example: This test is easy.
practice: English numbers are easy for me now.
The second test is easier than the first test.
Easy, easier, the easiest: the y becomes i.
It is easy to cook rice.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor one easy thing and one difficult thing for you. True or made up is fine.

words.meaning: Not easy. You need help, or a lot of time.
words.example: This question is difficult.
practice: Is English difficult? Some words are.
The last test was more difficult than the first test.
Difficult is a long word: more difficult, the most difficult.
Driving in the city is difficult.
words.tutor: Say the most difficult word in this unit for you. Ask the tutor to say it slowly, then say it back three times.

words.meaning: Not near. You need a long time to go there.
words.example: The station is far from my home.
practice: Is the bank far? No, it is near the park.
The market is far, but the shop is near.
The city is further than the village.
Far, further, the furthest: far changes.
words.tutor: Name two places to the tutor, like a shop and a park. Real or made up is fine. Say which one is near and which one is further.

words.meaning: Here, you can't get hurt easily.
words.example: This street is safe at night.
practice: Is the park safe in the evening?
A train is safer than a bike on a busy road.
Your phone is safe in the bag.
Safe, safer, the safest.
words.starter: This street is safe. It has …
words.tutor: Tell the tutor about a street near you, real or made up. Say one thing that makes it safe or dangerous.

words.meaning: Not safe. You can get hurt.
words.example: This road is dangerous. Walk carefully.
practice: A storm can be dangerous.
The big road is more dangerous than the small road.
Dangerous is a long word: more dangerous, the most dangerous.
It is dangerous to cross here. Use the bridge.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor one dangerous thing on a road and one safe thing. Ask it to check the two lines.

words.meaning: Nice to sit on or sleep on. It does not hurt.
words.example: This chair is very comfortable.
practice: My bed is more comfortable than the floor.
The train is more comfortable than the bus.
Comfortable: say it in three parts, comf-ta-ble.
Are you comfortable? Yes, thanks.
words.starter: The most comfortable thing in my home is …
words.tutor: Say comfortable to the tutor three times. Ask it if you said three parts, comf-ta-ble, and not four.

words.meaning: Just like the other one.
words.example: We have got the same phone.
practice: Your bag and my bag are the same.
The bus and the train leave at the same time.
Is it the same price? Yes, it is 40.
Say the before same: the same bag.
words.starter: … and I have got the same …
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to name two things, like two cups. Say one thing that is the same about them, with the same.

words.meaning: Not the same.
words.example: The two bags are different colours.
practice: My phone is different from your phone.
The two shops have different prices.
The city and the village are very different.
Different, not the same: one is red, one is blue.
words.tutor: Compare two things near you with the tutor. Say one thing that is the same and one thing that is different.

words.meaning: Not loudly. It makes a very small sound.
words.example: Please talk quietly in the library.
practice: The baby is sleeping. Close the door quietly.
She speaks quietly. I can't hear her.
Quiet, quietly: add -ly.
He walked quietly to the door.
words.tutor: Say one line to the tutor loudly, then say it quietly. Ask it to write both lines with the how word at the end.

words.meaning: Good, for how you do something.
words.example: She cooks well.
practice: I can speak English well now.
He drives well. He is a good driver.
Good is for a thing. Well is for how you do it.
Well, better, the best: I sing better than my brother.
Did you sleep well?
words.tutor: Tell the tutor three things you do well, true or made up. Ask it to tell you if you said good where well is right.

words.meaning: A lot, and for a long time.
words.example: I work hard every day.
practice: She studies hard for her test.
It is raining hard. Take an umbrella.
Hard stays hard. Not hardly.
We worked hard in the garden on Saturday.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor what you work hard at. It can be at school or at work. Ask it to check you said hard, not hardly.

words.meaning: Not well.
words.example: I sing badly.
practice: He drives badly. He is a dangerous driver.
I slept badly. The bed was not comfortable.
Bad, badly: add -ly.
Badly, worse, the worst: I cook worse than my sister.
words.tutor: Say one thing you do well and one you do badly. True or made up is fine. Ask the tutor to check you said well and badly, not good and bad.

words.meaning: Ten hundreds: 1,000.
words.example: A kilo is a thousand grams.
practice: The price is 1,000. That is expensive!
One thousand, not one thousands.
A thousand people live in the village.
Nine hundred and ninety-nine, then a thousand.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to say five numbers between 100 and 1,000. Write each one in numbers, then check with the tutor.

words.meaning: How big a thing is.
words.example: What size is this bag?
practice: This bag is the right size for me.
The two rooms are the same size.
Small or large: what size do you want?
I need a larger size, please.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor the size of a room, a bag or a table. It can be real or made up. Use small, large, bigger or smaller.

words.meaning: We say how heavy a thing is in kilos.
words.example: A kilo of rice, please.
practice: The bag of rice is five kilos.
How much is a kilo of apples?
Two kilos, not two kilo.
My bag is heavier. It is ten kilos.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for a short shopping list with kilos. Read it back and say how much you need of each thing.

words.meaning: We say how long or tall a thing is in metres.
words.example: The door is two metres tall.
practice: My room is four metres long.
The table is one and a half metres long.
The bridge is 500 metres long.
A hundred centimetres make a metre.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor how long a room or a table is, in metres. A made-up number is fine. Ask it to say the line back to you.

words.meaning: A small part of a metre. There are 100 centimetres in a metre.
words.example: This pen is 15 centimetres long.
practice: My phone is 14 centimetres long.
The box is 30 centimetres tall.
One metre is one hundred centimetres.
The glass is 12 centimetres tall.
words.tutor: Look at a pen or a phone near you. Tell the tutor how long it is in centimetres. Ask it how to say the number.

words.meaning: We say how much water or milk there is in litres.
words.example: I drink two litres of water every day.
practice: A litre of milk, please.
The bottle is one litre.
How much is the two-litre bottle?
This bottle is larger. It is five litres.
words.starter: I drink … litres of water every day.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor about a big bottle and a small bottle. Say which bottle has more litres, and how many.

words.meaning: A very small part of a kilo. There are 1,000 grams in a kilo.
words.example: This phone is 200 grams.
practice: A small bag of tea is 250 grams.
500 grams of meat, please.
Grams are for light things. Kilos are for heavy things.
My phone is lighter. It is 150 grams.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor three light things and how many grams they are. Made-up numbers are fine.

words.meaning: Look at two things. See what is the same and what is different.
words.example: Compare the two prices.
practice: I compare the prices, then I pay.
Compare the bus and the train. Which one is cheaper?
We compared the two phones.
Compare, compared: add -d.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you two things to compare. Say two lines: one with -er and one with more.

words.meaning: Look at two or more things, then take the one you want.
words.example: Which one do you choose?
practice: I choose the green bag. It is lighter.
It is difficult to choose.
You can choose any chair.
Choose one answer from the list.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you two things with a price and a size. Choose one and say two things about it.

grammar.title: Cheaper, the cheapest; more and the most
grammar.explanation:
Compare two things: add -er, then say than.
A long word takes more: more expensive.
For three or more, use the -est or the most.
grammar.rule:
Two things:
The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
My bag is lighter than your bag.
The city is larger than the village.

Long words take more:
The taxi is more expensive than the bus.
A bed is more comfortable than the floor.

Three or more:
The bus is the cheapest.
The taxi is the most expensive.

Spelling:
large, larger, the largest
big, bigger, the biggest: two g
heavy, heavier, the heaviest: y becomes i
easy, easier, the easiest

Long words: expensive, difficult, dangerous, comfortable.
grammar.workedExample:
The bus is 3. The taxi is 20.
1. The bus is 3. That is cheap.
2. Cheap is a short word: add -er. Cheaper.
3. Add than, then the other thing.
4. The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
5. Now the taxi. Expensive is a long word: more expensive.
6. The taxi is more expensive than the bus.
7. Check: -er or more, never both.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to put more and -er together.
No: The bus is more cheaper.
Yes: The bus is cheaper.
It is easy to leave out than.
No: The bus is cheaper the taxi.
Yes: The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
grammar.tip: Short word: -er. Long word: more. Never both.
grammar.practice:
Write the right form of the word.
1. A bike is ___ than a car. (cheap)
2. My new chair is ___ than my old chair. (comfortable)
3. This box is ___ than that box. (heavy)
4. The city is ___ than the village. (large)
5. The big road is ___ than the small road. (dangerous)
6. Three bags: the green one is the ___. (light)
7. Three phones: this one is the ___. (expensive)
8. The first test is easy. The second test is ___. (easy)
grammar.answers:
1. cheaper  2. more comfortable  3. heavier  4. larger  5. more dangerous  6. lightest  7. most expensive  8. easier
Wrong on 3 or 8? The y becomes i: heavier, easier.
Wrong on 7? Three or more, and a long word: the most expensive.

grammar.title: Good, better, best; bad, worse, worst
grammar.explanation:
Good and bad do not take -er or more.
They change to new words.
Use them with I think to say what you think.
grammar.rule:
good, better, the best
bad, worse, the worst
far, further, the furthest

The blue bag is good.
The black bag is better.
The red bag is the best.

This café is bad.
That café is worse.
The café on the corner is the worst.

Say what you think:
I think the black bag is better.
I think this café is the best.
grammar.workedExample:
Three phones. Phone 1 is good. Phone 2 is very good. Phone 3 is very, very good.
1. Two phones: use better.
2. Phone 2 is better than phone 1.
3. Three phones: use the best.
4. Phone 3 is the best.
5. Check: no -er on good. Not gooder. Not more good.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to make good like cheap.
No: This phone is gooder.
No: This phone is more good.
Yes: This phone is better.
No: It is the baddest.
Yes: It is the worst.
grammar.tip: Say them in threes: good, better, best. Bad, worse, worst.
grammar.practice:
Write better, the best, worse, the worst or further.
1. Café 1 is good. Café 2 is ___ than café 1.
2. This is ___ film of the year. No film is better.
3. The weather is bad today. Yesterday it was ___.
4. This road has a lot of accidents. It is ___ road in the city.
5. My English is ___ now than last year.
6. The market is far. The station is ___.
7. Three pens: the red one is ___.
8. The storm today is ___ than the storm last week. It is very bad.
grammar.answers:
1. better  2. the best  3. worse  4. the worst  5. better  6. further  7. the best  8. worse
Wrong on 7? Three or more: the best, not better.
Wrong on 8? Two storms: worse. The worst is for three or more.

grammar.title: Well, hard, badly: a good cook cooks well
grammar.explanation:
A how word says how you do something.
Most end in -ly: quiet, quietly.
Good changes to well. Hard stays hard.
grammar.rule:
the person, then how:
a quiet person: she talks quietly
a bad singer: he sings badly
a good cook: she cooks well
a hard worker: he works hard

good: a thing or a person
well: how you do it

hard stays hard.
Not hardly. Hardly is a different word.

The how word goes after the doing word, or at the end:
I speak English well.
She works hard every day.
Talk quietly, please.

well, better, the best
badly, worse, the worst
She sings better than me.
grammar.workedExample:
Omar is a good driver. How does he drive?
1. Good is for the person: a good driver.
2. For how he drives, good changes to well.
3. Well goes after drives.
4. He drives well.
5. Check: not He drives good. Not He drives goodly.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use good for how you do something.
No: She cooks good.
Yes: She cooks well.
It is easy to add -ly to hard.
No: He works hardly.
Yes: He works hard.
grammar.practice:
Write the how word.
1. Hana is a quiet person. She talks ___.
2. Ben is a good swimmer. He swims ___.
3. Mia is a bad cook. She cooks ___.
4. Leo is a hard worker. He works ___.
5. Sam is a careful driver. He drives ___.
6. Eva is a good singer. She sings ___.
7. The baby is sleeping. Please talk ___.
8. Ivan is a bad driver. He drives ___.
grammar.answers:
1. quietly  2. well  3. badly  4. hard  5. carefully  6. well  7. quietly  8. badly
Wrong on 2 or 6? Good changes to well: he swims well.
Wrong on 4? Hard stays hard: he works hard.

grammar.title: How much is it? Some, any, many, much, no
grammar.explanation:
Many is for things you can count. Much is for things you can't count.
A lot of is for both.
Some is for yes sentences. Any is for questions and not.
grammar.rule:
You can count them:
How many eggs do you need?
I need six eggs.
There aren't many eggs.

You can't count it:
How much rice do you need?
I need a kilo.
There isn't much milk.

For both, in a yes sentence:
I need a lot of eggs.
I need a lot of rice.

some and any:
I've got some bread.
Have you got any bread?
I haven't got any bread.

no is not any:
There is no milk.
There are no eggs.

Prices:
How much is it? It is 25.
How much are they? They are 40.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to ask about milk.
1. Can you count milk? No. You count litres, not milk.
2. So use much, not many.
3. How much milk do you need?
4. Answer: I need two litres. Or: I need a lot of milk.
5. Check: much with milk, rice, water and money. Many with eggs, cups and people.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use many with a thing you can't count.
No: How many money is it?
Yes: How much money is it? Or: How much is it?
It is easy to use some with not.
No: I haven't got some eggs.
Yes: I haven't got any eggs.
grammar.tip: Count it: many. Can't count it: much. A price: how much.
grammar.practice:
Write some, any, many, much, a lot of or no.
1. How ___ apples do you want? Six, please.
2. How ___ water do you drink every day?
3. Is there ___ milk in the fridge?
4. There are ___ people at the market. It is very busy.
5. I've got ___ bread. Do you want it?
6. We haven't got ___ time. The train is at six.
7. There is ___ sugar. The bag is empty.
8. How ___ is the red bag? It is 45.
grammar.answers:
1. many  2. much  3. any  4. a lot of  5. some  6. much (any is right too)  7. no  8. much
Wrong on 8? For a price, it is always How much.
Wrong on 4? People: you can count them. In a yes sentence, say a lot of.

grammar.title: Which one is yours? This one
grammar.explanation:
Which one? asks a person to choose.
Say one. Do not say the thing again.
This one is near you. That one is not near you.
grammar.rule:
Which one is yours?
This one. (It is near me.)
That one. (It is not near me.)
The blue one.
The small one.

Which one do you want?
That one, please.

Which one is cheaper?
This one is cheaper than that one.

Two or more: ones
Which ones are yours? The black ones.

Which bag is yours? Which one is yours? Both are right.
grammar.workedExample:
You are in a shop. There are two bags. You want the bag near you.
1. The shop asks: Which one do you want?
2. The bag is near you: this.
3. Say one. Do not say bag again.
4. This one, please.
5. Check: one after this, and no bag.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to leave out one.
No: I want the blue.
Yes: I want the blue one.
It is easy to put the thing in the wrong place.
No: Which is yours bag?
Yes: Which bag is yours? Or: Which one is yours?
grammar.tip: Which one? This one. That one. The red one.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing word.
1. Two phones. Yours is in your hand. Which one is yours? ___ one.
2. Two bags. You want the bag that is not near you. ___ one, please.
3. Two keys. Yours is small. Which one is yours? The small ___.
4. You ask about two bikes: ___ one is cheaper?
5. Three cups. You want the red cup. I want the red ___.
6. Two umbrellas. They are yours. Which ___ are yours? The black ones.
grammar.answers:
1. This  2. That  3. one  4. Which  5. one  6. ones
Wrong on 1 or 2? This is near you. That is not near you.
Wrong on 6? Two or more things: ones.

grammar.title: Up to a thousand: a hundred and five
grammar.explanation:
After hundred, say and: a hundred and five.
After a number, hundred and thousand have no s.
Ten hundreds is a thousand.
grammar.rule:
100: a hundred, or one hundred
105: a hundred and five
250: two hundred and fifty
399: three hundred and ninety-nine
600: six hundred
812: eight hundred and twelve
1,000: a thousand, or one thousand

two hundred, not two hundreds

The price is 450: four hundred and fifty.
The bag is 750 grams: seven hundred and fifty grams.
grammar.workedExample:
Read 365.
1. Look at the first number: 3. Say three hundred.
2. Say and.
3. Look at the last two numbers: 65. Say sixty-five.
4. Three hundred and sixty-five.
5. Check: no s on hundred. And after hundred.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to add s to hundred.
No: three hundreds.
Yes: three hundred.
It is easy to leave out and.
No: two hundred fifty.
Yes: two hundred and fifty.
grammar.tip: Hundred, then and, then the rest.
grammar.answers:
1. a hundred and twenty  2. two hundred and eight  3. four hundred and fifteen  4. seven hundred and thirty  5. nine hundred and ninety-nine  6. a thousand  7. five hundred and sixty  8. three hundred and one
One hundred and twenty and one thousand are right too.
Wrong on 2 or 8? No tens here. Say hundred, and, then one number: two hundred and eight.

readings.title: Two Bags for a Trip
readings.setting: Two friends compare two bags in a shop.
readings.passage:
Yara: Look at these two bags. Which one do you like?
Dan: I like the black one. It is larger than the green one.
Yara: Yes, but it is heavier. The green one is 800 grams. The black one is 2 kilos.
Dan: How much is the green one?
Yara: It is 45. The black one is 70.
Dan: So the green one is cheaper and lighter.
Yara: I think the green one is better for a trip.
Dan: I don't think so. I think the black one is better. You can carry a lot of things in it.
Yara: OK. I choose the green one, and you can get the black one!

readings.title: Bus, Train or Taxi?
readings.setting: An information page for people who visit a village.
readings.passage:
Bus, train or taxi? You want to go to the city. Compare them.
The bus is the cheapest. It is 120, and the trip is two hours.
The train is more expensive. It is 250, and the trip is one hour. It is the most comfortable.
The taxi is the most expensive. It is 900, and the trip is 50 minutes.
The bus and the train leave at the same time: 8 o'clock.
All three are safe.
For a cheap trip, choose the bus.
We think the train is the best. It is not very expensive, and it is comfortable.

readings.title: The Corner Shop Price List
readings.setting: A list on the wall of a corner shop.
readings.passage:
CORNER SHOP: PRICES THIS WEEK
Rice, 1 kilo: 120
Rice, 5 kilos: 550
Milk, 1 litre: 90
Milk, 2 litres: 160
Tea, 250 grams: 300
Sugar, 500 grams: 110
Water, 5 litres: 200
Bags: small 20, large 35
Sorry, no eggs this week.
Large bags are stronger than small bags.
Big bags of rice are heavy. Ask us. We can help you carry them.
Open every day, from 7 in the morning to 9 at night.

comprehension.why: Dan says: I like the black one. It is larger than the green one.
Yara says: The green one is 800 grams. The black one is 2 kilos.

comprehension.q: Dan says the green bag is cheaper. How does he know?
comprehension.a: Yara tells him the prices. The green bag is 45 and the black bag is 70.
comprehension.why: Yara says: It is 45. The black one is 70. 45 is smaller than 70, so the green one is cheaper.

comprehension.q: Which bag does Yara think is better for a trip? Which one does Dan think is better?
comprehension.a: Yara thinks the green one is better. Dan thinks the black one is better.
comprehension.why: Yara says: I think the green one is better for a trip. Dan says: I think the black one is better. The words I think tell you what a person thinks.

comprehension.q: Which is the cheapest: the bus, the train or the taxi?
comprehension.why: The text says: The bus is the cheapest. It is 120.

comprehension.q: The bus and the train leave at the same time. What time is that?
comprehension.why: The text says: The bus and the train leave at the same time: 8 o'clock. The same time means one time for both.

comprehension.q: Which one does the writer think is the best, and why?
comprehension.a: The train. It is not very expensive, and it is comfortable.
comprehension.why: The last two lines: We think the train is the best. It is not very expensive, and it is comfortable.

comprehension.q: You need 2 litres of milk. Which is cheaper: one 2-litre milk, or two 1-litre milks?
comprehension.a: One 2-litre milk. It is 160. Two 1-litre milks are 180.
comprehension.why: The list says: Milk, 1 litre: 90. Milk, 2 litres: 160. 90 and 90 is 180, and 160 is cheaper.

comprehension.q: You want eggs. Can you get them at this shop this week?
comprehension.why: The list says: Sorry, no eggs this week. No eggs means there aren't any eggs.

comprehension.q: You get 5 kilos of rice. It is very heavy. What can you do?
comprehension.a: Ask the shop. They can help you carry it.
comprehension.why: The last line says: Big bags of rice are heavy. Ask us. We can help you carry them.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Cheaper, better, the best
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
My bag is lighter than your bag.
The train is more comfortable than the bus.
The taxi is the most expensive.
This café is good. That café is better.
I think the café on the corner is the best.
Tap the mic. Say the 6 lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: than after -er and more? The before -est and most? Better, not gooder?
speaking.tutor: Say the six lines to the tutor. Ask it to find any line with more and -er together, like more cheaper.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — How I do things
speaking.instructions:
Say 5 lines about you.
I ___ well.
I ___ badly.
I work hard at ___.
I talk quietly in ___.
I ___ better than my ___.
Pick from: cook, sing, drive, swim, draw, speak English.
At school, at work or at home: all are fine.
It can be true or made up.
Tap the mic. Say it. Tap again. Listen.
Check: well, not good? Hard, not hardly? Five lines?
speaking.instructionsSpeech:
Say 5 lines about you.
I … well.
I … badly.
I work hard at …
I talk quietly in …
I … better than my …
Pick from: cook, sing, drive, swim, draw, speak English.
At school, at work or at home: all are fine.
It can be true or made up.
Tap the mic. Say it. Tap again. Listen.
Check: well, not good? Hard, not hardly? Five lines?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your five lines. Ask it to ask you How do you …? about two more things, and answer with a how word.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Which one does she like?
speaking.instructions:
Listen to Lena and Omar. They compare two phones.
Lena: I like the black phone. It is lighter.
Omar: I think the white phone is better. It is larger.
Lena: But the white one is 400. The black one is 250.
Omar: Yes, the black one is cheaper. But I choose the white one.
Now answer. Say a full line.
1. Which phone does Lena like? She likes ___.
2. Which phone does Omar think is better? He thinks ___.
3. Which phone is cheaper? The ___ is cheaper.
Tap the mic. Say the 3 answers. Tap again. Listen.
Now check. Read the four lines again.
Find I like and I think. They tell you what a person thinks.
Find the two prices. Which number is smaller?
Do your answers match?
speaking.instructionsSpeech:
Listen to Lena and Omar. They compare two phones.
Lena: I like the black phone. It is lighter.
Omar: I think the white phone is better. It is larger.
Lena: But the white one is 400. The black one is 250.
Omar: Yes, the black one is cheaper. But I choose the white one.
Now answer. Say a full line.
1. Which phone does Lena like? She likes …
2. Which phone does Omar think is better? He thinks …
3. Which phone is cheaper? The … is cheaper.
Tap the mic. Say the 3 answers. Tap again. Listen.
Now check. Read the four lines again.
Find I like and I think. They tell you what a person thinks.
Find the two prices. Which number is smaller?
Do your answers match?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for two short lines from two people. Each person likes a different thing. Say which one each person likes, and which words told you.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Thirteen or thirty?
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat.
13, thirteen. 30, thirty.
15, fifteen. 50, fifty.
Thirteen: the end is long and strong.
Thirty: the start is strong.
115: a hundred and fifteen.
150: a hundred and fifty.
In a hundred and fifty, and is short and quick.
999: nine hundred and ninety-nine.
1,000: a thousand.
Now say these prices: 118, 180, 415, 450, 760.
Tap the mic. Say the 5 numbers. Tap again. Listen.
Check: a strong end on eighteen and fifteen? And after hundred? No s on hundred?
speaking.tutor: Say ten numbers between 100 and 1,000 to the tutor. Ask it to write what it hears, then compare with your list.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — How much? How many?
speaking.instructions:
Read A. Say B.
1. A: How many eggs do you need? B: I need six eggs.
2. A: How much rice do you need? B: I need two kilos.
3. A: Have you got any milk? B: Yes, I've got some milk.
4. A: Is there any sugar? B: No, there is no sugar.
5. A: How much is this bag? B: It is 35.
6. A: Are there many people at the market? B: Yes, there are a lot of people.
Tap the mic. Say the 6 B lines. Tap again. Listen.
Now say them for you. Change the numbers and the food.
Check: many with eggs and people? Much with rice? Some in a yes line, any in a question?
A friend can say A. No one with you? Say A and B.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be a person at a market. Ask it How much …? and How many …? questions, and answer its questions too.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Which one do you want?
speaking.instructions:
You are in a shop. You want a bag.
Listen. Say your lines.
Shop: Hello! Can I help you?
You: Yes, please. I want a bag for a trip.
Shop: We have got two. Which one do you want?
You: Which one is lighter?
Shop: That one. It is 800 grams.
You: How much is it?
Shop: That one is 45. This one is 60.
You: OK. I choose that one, please.
Shop: Here you are.
You: Thanks. Goodbye!
Tap the mic. Say your lines. Tap again. Listen.
Check: Which one? How much is it? One after that?
Now say it again, but choose this one. It is 60.
A friend can read the shop lines. No one with you? Read them and answer.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be a shop assistant. It has three bags, with different prices and sizes. Ask Which one is …? two times, then choose one.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Compare two things
writing.prompt:
Choose two things, like a bike and a car, or two bags.
Write 4 lines to compare them.
Use -er or more, and than.
They can be true or made up.
writing.model:
A bike is cheaper than a car.
A bike is lighter than a car.
A car is more expensive than a bike.
A car is more comfortable than a bike.
writing.criteria:
4 lines, each with than.
At least 2 lines with -er and 1 line with more.
No line has more and -er together.
A capital letter and a full stop in each line.
writing.support:
Start with the price. Which one is cheaper?
Write: The ___ is cheaper than the ___.
Now change cheaper to lighter. That is line 2.
writing.extension: Add a fifth line about three things: The bus is the cheapest.

writing.title: Writing 2 — How I do things
writing.prompt:
Write 4 lines about how you do things.
Use well, badly, hard and quietly, one in each line.
They can be true or made up.
writing.model:
I cook well.
I sing badly.
I study hard in the evening.
I read quietly in the library.
writing.criteria:
4 lines: well, badly, hard, quietly.
Well, not good. Hard, not hardly.
The how word comes after the doing word, or at the end.
writing.support:
Copy the model.
Change the doing word only: cook, sing, study, read.
Say each line out loud. Does it sound like the model?
writing.extension: Add a line with better: I cook better than my brother.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A shopping list
writing.prompt:
You want to make dinner for four people.
Write a shopping list. Say how much or how many you need.
Then write 2 lines with some and any.
writing.model:
SHOPPING LIST
2 kilos of rice
6 eggs
2 litres of milk
500 grams of meat
I need some bread.
I don't need any sugar.
writing.criteria:
4 lines with a number.
Kilos, grams or litres in 3 of them.
An s on kilos, grams and litres after 2 or more.
1 line with some. 1 line with any and not.
writing.support:
Look at the price list in Reading 3.
Copy 4 things from it. Change the numbers.
Then copy the some line and the any line from the model.
writing.extension: Add a question for the shop: How much is a kilo of rice?

writing.title: Writing 4 — Which one do you choose?
writing.prompt:
Look at the bags in Reading 3, or think of two things you want.
Write 5 lines. Compare the two things.
Then say what you think, and which one you choose.
writing.model:
The small bag is 20. The large bag is 35.
The small bag is cheaper than the large bag.
The large bag is heavier, but it is stronger.
I think the large bag is better for a lot of shopping.
I choose the large one.
writing.criteria:
5 lines.
2 lines compare, with -er or more.
1 line with I think and better or the best.
1 line with I choose and one.
A capital letter and a full stop in each line.
writing.support:
Write the two prices first, like line 1 of the model.
Then copy line 2 and change the words.
Last, write: I choose the ___ one.
writing.extension: Add a line for a friend: But you can choose the ___ one. It is ___.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Cheaper or the cheapest?
activities.instructions:
Look at the three phones.
Phone 1: 150. It is 200 grams.
Phone 2: 300. It is 180 grams.
Phone 3: 600. It is 160 grams.
Write the right word.
1. Phone 1 is ___ than phone 2. (cheap)
2. Phone 2 is ___ than phone 1. (expensive)
3. Phone 3 is the ___. (expensive)
4. Phone 1 is the ___. (cheap)
5. Phone 3 is ___ than phone 2. (light)
6. Phone 1 is the ___. (heavy)
7. Phone 3 is the ___. (light)
8. Phone 1 is ___ than phone 3. (heavy)
activities.answers:
1. cheaper  2. more expensive  3. most expensive  4. cheapest  5. lighter  6. heaviest  7. lightest  8. heavier
Wrong on 6 or 8? Heavy: the y becomes i. Heavier, heaviest.
Wrong on 2 or 3? Expensive is a long word: more, the most.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 1 and do it again.
activities.solo: Write your answers on paper. Check with the key. Count the right ones.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Better or the best?
activities.instructions:
Write the right word.
1. This café is good, but that café is (better / gooder).
2. It is (the best / the most good) film this year.
3. The weather is bad today. Yesterday it was (badder / worse).
4. This is (the worst / the baddest) road in the city.
5. My English is (better / more good) now.
6. The station is (further / more far) than the market.
7. Three cafés: this one is (the best / better).
8. Two tests: the first was bad, and the second was (worse / the worst).
activities.answers:
1. better  2. the best  3. worse  4. the worst  5. better  6. further  7. the best  8. worse
Wrong on 7? Three or more: the best.
Wrong on 8? Two things: worse. The worst is for three or more.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 2 and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each line out loud with your word. Write the word. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Good or well?
activities.instructions:
Write good, well, badly, hard or quietly.
1. Sam is a ___ cook. He cooks ___.
2. Eva sings ___. Her songs are not good.
3. The baby is sleeping. Please close the door ___.
4. Nadia studies ___ every evening.
5. Is the food ___? Yes, it is very good.
6. He drives ___. He is a dangerous driver.
7. I didn't sleep ___. The bed was not comfortable.
8. It is raining ___. Take an umbrella.
activities.answers:
1. good, well  2. badly  3. quietly  4. hard  5. good  6. badly  7. well  8. hard
There are 9 gaps. Number 1 has two.
Wrong on 1? A good cook is the person. Cooks well is how.
Wrong on 5? Food is a thing: good. Well is for how you do it.
8 or 9 right: good.
7 or less: read Pattern 3 and do it again.
activities.solo: Write each word on paper. Read the full line out loud. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Much, many, some, any, no
activities.instructions:
Write the right word.
1. How (much / many) eggs do you want?
2. How (much / many) water is in the bottle?
3. I've got (some / any) apples. Do you want one?
4. Have you got (some / any) money with you?
5. There isn't (much / many) milk. Get two litres.
6. There are (no / any) eggs. The box is empty.
7. There are (a lot of / much) people in the park.
8. How (much / many) is this phone? It is 300.
activities.answers:
1. many  2. much  3. some  4. any  5. much  6. no  7. a lot of  8. much
Wrong on 8? For a price, it is always How much.
Wrong on 6? Any needs not: There aren't any eggs. Without not, say no: There are no eggs.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 4 and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each line out loud with your word. Write the word. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Match the word
activities.instructions:
Match 1 to 8 with a to h.
1. heavy
2. far
3. dangerous
4. size
5. litre
6. gram
7. same
8. comfortable
a. Not near.
b. How big a thing is.
c. Nice to sit on. It does not hurt.
d. Not safe.
e. You can't carry it easily.
f. For milk and water.
g. Just like the other one.
h. A very small part of a kilo.
activities.answers:
1e  2a  3d  4b  5f  6h  7g  8c
Check 5 and 6: a litre is for milk and water. A gram is a small part of a kilo.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: go back to Words, listen again, and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each word out loud. Write the letter. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Write the number
activities.instructions:
Part A. Write the number in words.
1. 140
2. 215
3. 370
4. 508
5. 999
Part B. Write the number.
6. six hundred and twelve
7. a thousand
8. four hundred and forty
activities.answers:
1. a hundred and forty  2. two hundred and fifteen  3. three hundred and seventy  4. five hundred and eight  5. nine hundred and ninety-nine  6. 612  7. 1,000  8. 440
One hundred and forty is right too.
Wrong on 4? 508 has no tens: five hundred and eight.
Wrong on 8? Forty is 40, and fourteen is 14.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 6 and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each number out loud first. Then write it. Check each word with the key.

quizzes.q: The bus is 3. The taxi is 20. The bus is ___ than the taxi.
quizzes.why: Cheap is a short word, so add -er: cheaper. Cheap takes -er, not more cheap. Cheapest is for three or more. More cheaper uses more and -er together.

quizzes.q: This chair is ___ than that chair.
quizzes.why: Comfortable is a long word, so use more: more comfortable. Comfortabler adds -er to a long word. The most is for three or more. Comfortable alone does not go with than.

quizzes.q: Three bags: 20, 35 and 50. The bag for 20 is ___.
quizzes.why: Three bags, so use the -est: the cheapest. Cheaper is for two things. Cheap is short, so not the most cheap. Cheap than has no -er.

quizzes.q: Café 1 is good. Café 2 is very good. Café 2 is ___ than café 1.
quizzes.why: Good changes: good, better, the best. Gooder and more good are not words we use. The best is for three or more, and it does not go with than.

quizzes.q: It is very, very bad weather. It is the ___ weather of the year.
quizzes.why: Bad changes: bad, worse, the worst. The whole year is more than two things, so the worst. Worse is for two things. Baddest and most bad are not right.

quizzes.q: Omar is a good driver. He drives ___.
quizzes.why: For how he drives, good changes to well. Good is for the person: a good driver. Goodly is not a word we use. Better than needs a second thing after it.
Hard stays hard, and it goes after works. Hardly is a different word. She hard works has the wrong order. In She is work, take out is.
You can't count rice, so use much: How much rice? Many is for things you can count, like eggs. Any does not go after how. A lot needs of: a lot of rice.

quizzes.q: The fridge is empty. There is ___ milk.
quizzes.why: No means not any: There is no milk. Any needs not: There isn't any milk. Some says there is milk. Many is for things you can count.

quizzes.q: Two pens. Yours is in your hand. Which one is yours?
quizzes.why: The pen is in your hand, so it is near you: this one. That one is not near you. Those ones is for two or more. Which one is the question, not the answer.
250 is two hundred, and, fifty. Hundred has no s after two. Twenty-five hundred is 2,500. Two hundred and fifteen is 215: fifteen, not fifty.

quizzes.q: You need 2 litres of milk. 1 litre is 90. The 2-litre bottle is 160. Which is cheaper?
quizzes.why: 90 and 90 is 180. 160 is smaller than 180, so the 2-litre bottle is cheaper. 180 and 160 are not the same. Milk is in litres, not kilos.

teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. If you are helping, listen to the recordings together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence. Speaking 3 is a listening check: the learner answers, then re-reads the four lines to find I like and I think, so the check comes from the text rather than from a key.

teacherNotes.type: The two errors worth your attention
teacherNotes.note: Two slips carry most of the unit: more and -er together (more cheaper, more better), and good where well is needed (she cooks good). When you hear the first, ask whether the word is short or long; when you hear the second, ask whether it describes the person or how they do it. The tips on Patterns 1 and 3 are the whole rule. Far is given as far, further, the furthest; farther is also correct and should not be marked wrong.

Prices are numbers with no currency, and none of them is meant as a real price anywhere. Measures are in kilos, grams, metres, centimetres and litres; a learner who meets other measures at home loses nothing by learning these. No task asks what the learner earns, owns or spends, and every choice task can be done with made-up things.

Reasons are given as a second sentence (It is lighter.) rather than with because, which is Unit 19. Questions such as How far? and How long? are Unit 18, so this unit states sizes and weights instead of asking for them. I think and I don't think so are used as fixed chunks for opinion. Much and many are kept to questions and lines with not; yes sentences use a lot of, which is how most speakers say it.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task is scored by it alone. The learner is told that made-up answers are fine. Keep that wording, and never ask the learner to give the tutor real personal details, prices they pay or where they live.

selfAssessment.statement: I can write: The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
I can say which one I think is better, or the best.
I can say how I do things: well, hard, badly, quietly.
I can ask How much is it? and How many do you need?
I can ask Which one is yours? and answer This one.
I can read and say a price or a size up to 1,000.
I can hear which one a person likes or thinks is better.

assignment.title: Which one is better?
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Tap the mic. Compare two things you know: two bags, two phones or two places. Say how much each one is. Say which one is cheaper and which one you think is better. Say which one you choose.
2. Write the 5 lines of Writing 4.
You can use made-up things and made-up prices.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written text
